items.title: Patel: From Barrister to 'Sardar'
items.body:
**In one line** — How a successful lawyer gave up his career for the freedom struggle and, through two peasant movements, became 'Sardar' (the leader).

**Why it is asked** — Examiners love the *order* of Patel's two satyagrahas (Kheda before Bardoli) and the fact that the title 'Sardar' came from Bardoli, not Kheda.

## The story

- **Who:** **Vallabhbhai Patel** (born 1875, Nadiad, Gujarat) trained as a **barrister** (a courtroom lawyer) in London and built a thriving practice in **Ahmedabad**.
- **Turning point:** inspired by **Gandhi**, he gave up his legal career to join the national movement.
- **Kheda Satyagraha (1918):** his first mass campaign, with Gandhi. When crops failed and plague struck, the government still demanded full land revenue; Patel organised the Kheda peasants to **refuse payment** until relief was given. ('Satyagraha' = Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance.)
- **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928):** the government raised land revenue in Bardoli (Surat district) by about **22%**. Patel led a **disciplined no-tax campaign**; the peasants held firm, and the government was forced to **roll back the hike and return seized land**.
- **Result:** the grateful women of Bardoli gave Patel the title **'Sardar'** (chief/leader), and the victory made him a national figure and the Congress's master organiser.

## Picture it (timeline)

| Year | Campaign | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1918 | Kheda Satyagraha | First mass campaign with Gandhi |
| 1928 | Bardoli Satyagraha | Revenue hike rolled back → title 'Sardar' |

## Terms explained

- **Barrister** — a lawyer qualified to argue cases in higher courts.
- **Satyagraha** — Gandhi's non-violent resistance based on truth and moral pressure.
- **Land revenue** — the tax farmers paid to the government on their land.
- **Sardar** — 'chief' or 'leader'; Patel's lifelong honorific.

**Don't confuse** — the title **'Sardar' came from Bardoli (1928)**, NOT from Kheda (1918); Kheda was merely his first campaign.

**Remember it** — 'KB': **K**heda (1918) came before **B**ardoli (1928), and Bardoli made him Sardar.

**TL;DR**

- Patel: London-trained barrister who joined the struggle under Gandhi.
- Kheda (1918) = first mass campaign; Bardoli (1928) = no-tax win → title 'Sardar'.
- Became the Congress's chief organiser and disciplinarian.
keyPoints: Vallabhbhai Patel (b. 1875, Nadiad) was a London-trained barrister who joined the struggle under Gandhi.
Kheda Satyagraha (1918) was his first mass campaign against land revenue during crop failure.
Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) forced a rollback of a ~22% revenue hike.
The women of Bardoli gave him the title 'Sardar' after the 1928 success.
He was the Congress's foremost organiser and disciplinarian.
items.mnemonic: Order of Patel's campaigns: 'KB' = Kheda (1918) before Bardoli (1928).
items.source: NCERT & Britannica — Vallabhbhai Patel; Kheda & Bardoli Satyagrahas

items.title: Iron Man: Integration of the Princely States
items.body:
**In one line** — How Patel persuaded and pressured about 565 princely kingdoms to join India in 1947, saving the country from breaking into pieces.

**Why it is asked** — The number (~565 states), the tool (Instrument of Accession), and the duo (Patel + V.P. Menon) are high-frequency one-mark facts.

## The story

- **The problem:** when the British left in 1947, their **paramountcy** (overlordship over the princely states) **lapsed**. This left about **565 princely states** legally free to join **India**, join **Pakistan**, or stay **independent**. If many had stayed out, India would have been a patchwork full of holes — 'balkanisation'.
- **The machinery:** Patel headed the new **States Department** (set up July 1947), with **V.P. Menon** as his Secretary. He used a mix of **persuasion, appeals to patriotism, and firmness** to bring the rulers in.
- **The main tool — the Instrument of Accession:** a legal document by which a ruler handed over only **three subjects** to the Indian Union — **defence, external affairs and communications** — keeping internal matters for now. A **Standstill Agreement** kept existing arrangements running smoothly.
- **The sweetener:** rulers who joined were promised **privy purses** (annual government payments) and the right to keep their titles and privileges — these were finally **abolished in 1971**.
- **Result:** by 15 August 1947 the great majority had signed; only three hold-outs (Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir) remained, settled by 1948–49. For this, Patel earned the titles **'Iron Man of India'** and **'Bismarck of India'** (after the statesman who unified Germany).

## Picture it

```
British leave 1947 → paramountcy LAPSES → ~565 states free
        |
Patel + V.P. Menon (States Dept) → Instrument of Accession
        |                                   (defence + external affairs + communications)
   most states join by 15 Aug 1947 → only 3 hold-outs left
```

## Terms explained

- **Paramountcy** — the supreme overlordship the British Crown held over the princely states.
- **Instrument of Accession** — the legal deed by which a state joined India, ceding defence, external affairs and communications.
- **Standstill Agreement** — a stop-gap deal to keep existing administrative links running.
- **Privy purse** — an annual payment promised to a former ruler (abolished 1971).

**Don't confuse** — the Instrument of Accession transferred **only three subjects** at first, not full control; and 'Bismarck of India' refers to *unification*, not to any German link.

**Remember it** — 'Patel + Menon handed each raja a 3-subject form (defence, foreign affairs, communications).'

**TL;DR**

- 1947: ~565 states free to join India/Pakistan or stay independent.
- Patel (States Dept) + V.P. Menon used persuasion + firmness.
- Instrument of Accession ceded defence, external affairs, communications; privy purses promised (abolished 1971).
- Earned Patel 'Iron Man' / 'Bismarck of India'.
keyPoints: About 565 princely states were free to join India, join Pakistan, or stay independent in 1947.
Patel headed the States Department (1947), assisted by Secretary V.P. Menon.
The Instrument of Accession ceded defence, external affairs and communications to the Union.
Acceding rulers were promised privy purses (abolished in 1971).
Patel's success earned him the titles 'Iron Man' and 'Bismarck' of India.
items.source: NCERT 'Politics in India Since Independence' & Britannica — integration of princely states

items.title: The Three Hard Cases: Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir
items.body:
**In one line** — Most states joined India quietly; three refused and had to be handled by plebiscite, military action, or a last-minute accession.

**Why it is asked** — The match-the-state-with-its-method question is a near-certain MCQ; the trap is pairing 'Operation Polo' with Junagadh instead of Hyderabad.

## The story

Three states resisted joining India, each for a different reason, so each needed a different solution.

| State | The problem | How it was resolved |
|---|---|---|
| **Junagadh** | Its **Muslim Nawab acceded to Pakistan**, even though the people were **Hindu-majority** and the state had **no land link** to Pakistan | A **plebiscite (vote of the people) in February 1948** overwhelmingly chose India |
| **Hyderabad** | The **Nizam wanted independence**; his **Razakar** militia unleashed violence | **Operation Polo** — a 'Police Action' in **September 1948** — merged it into India |
| **Jammu & Kashmir** | **Maharaja Hari Singh** delayed deciding; then **Pakistani tribal raiders invaded (Oct 1947)** | He signed the **Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947**; India then sent troops |

- **Also note:** **Travancore** and **Bhopal** briefly talked of independence but soon acceded.
- Kashmir's accession came with a special arrangement (later **Article 370**) and remained politically disputed.

## Terms explained

- **Plebiscite** — a direct vote by the people to decide an issue (here, which country to join).
- **Operation Polo / Police Action** — the Indian army operation (Sept 1948) that integrated Hyderabad.
- **Razakars** — the Nizam's private militia that resisted integration.
- **Standstill / accession** — see the previous note; Kashmir acceded late, under invasion.

**Don't confuse** — **Operation Polo = Hyderabad**, NOT Junagadh (Junagadh = plebiscite). And the **tribal invasion was in Kashmir**, not Junagadh.

**Remember it** — 'J-H-K': **J**unagadh = plebiscite, **H**yderabad = Operation Polo, **K**ashmir = Instrument of Accession.

**TL;DR**

- Junagadh: Nawab chose Pakistan; Feb 1948 plebiscite chose India.
- Hyderabad: Nizam resisted; Operation Polo (Sept 1948).
- Kashmir: Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession (26 Oct 1947) after a tribal invasion.
- Travancore and Bhopal briefly sought independence, then acceded.
keyPoints: Junagadh: Nawab acceded to Pakistan; a February 1948 plebiscite chose India.
Hyderabad: integrated by Operation Polo (Police Action) in September 1948.
Jammu & Kashmir: Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947 after a tribal invasion.
Travancore and Bhopal briefly sought independence before acceding.
These three were the main exceptions to otherwise peaceful accession.
items.mnemonic: Trouble trio 'J-H-K' = Junagadh (plebiscite), Hyderabad (Operation Polo), Kashmir (Instrument of Accession).
items.source: NCERT & Britannica — Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir accession

items.title: Patel in Free India & His Legacy
items.body:
**In one line** — Patel's roles in the first government, his defence of the civil services as the nation's 'steel frame', and how India remembers him today.

**Why it is asked** — The 'steel frame' phrase, his offices, and the commemoration facts (Statue of Unity, Ekta Diwas, Bharat Ratna 1991) are frequent one-mark hooks.

## The story

- **His offices:** Patel was independent India's **first Home Minister** and **Deputy Prime Minister**, also holding the **States** and **Information & Broadcasting** portfolios.
- **The 'steel frame':** in the **Constituent Assembly** (the body that wrote the Constitution), Patel argued strongly for keeping the **All India Services** (the IAS and IPS). He called a strong, united, permanent service the **'steel frame'** that would hold the new nation together — which is why he is seen as the **patron of the modern IAS/IPS**.
- **Death and honours:** Patel died in **December 1950**. He was awarded the **Bharat Ratna in 1991** (posthumously — after his death).
- **Memorials:** the **Statue of Unity** (182 metres, at Kevadia, Gujarat — the **world's tallest statue**, inaugurated 2018) is dedicated to him, and his birth anniversary, **31 October**, is observed as **Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day)**.

## Picture it

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| First Home Minister & Deputy PM | 1947–1950 |
| 'Steel frame' | defended the All India Services (IAS/IPS) |
| Died | December 1950 |
| Bharat Ratna | 1991 (posthumous) |
| Statue of Unity | 182 m, Kevadia, world's tallest (2018) |
| Rashtriya Ekta Diwas | 31 October |

## Terms explained

- **Constituent Assembly** — the elected body that drafted India's Constitution (1946–49).
- **All India Services** — the central cadres (IAS, IPS) serving both the Union and the states.
- **'Steel frame'** — Patel's image for the civil services as the rigid structure holding India together.
- **Posthumous** — awarded after a person's death.

**Don't confuse** — the **Statue of Unity (182 m)** is for Patel; do not mix it up with any other memorial. And **Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (31 Oct)** marks Patel's *birth* anniversary.

**Remember it** — 'Patel = unity': Iron Man → Statue of **Unity** → National **Unity** Day (31 Oct).

**TL;DR**

- First Home Minister & Deputy PM; also States and I&B.
- Defended the All India Services as the 'steel frame'.
- Died Dec 1950; Bharat Ratna 1991 (posthumous).
- Statue of Unity (182 m, world's tallest); 31 October = Rashtriya Ekta Diwas.
keyPoints: Patel was India's first Home Minister and Deputy PM, also handling States and I&B.
He defended the All India Services as the 'steel frame' of India in the Constituent Assembly.
He died in December 1950 and received the Bharat Ratna (posthumous) in 1991.
The Statue of Unity (182 m, Kevadia, Gujarat) is the world's tallest statue.
31 October is observed as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day).
items.source: Government of India & Britannica — Vallabhbhai Patel; Statue of Unity; National Unity Day

items.title: Bose's Rise in the Congress & the Tripuri Split
items.body:
**In one line** — How Subhas Chandra Bose rose to lead the Congress twice, clashed with Gandhi at Tripuri, and then broke away to form the Forward Bloc.

**Why it is asked** — The two sessions (Haripura, Tripuri), the defeat of Gandhi's candidate, and Gandhi's famous remark are classic statement-based MCQ material.

## The story

- **Who:** **Subhas Chandra Bose** (born 1897, Cuttack) **resigned from the ICS** (the elite Indian Civil Service) to join the freedom struggle, becoming a protégé of the Bengal leader **Chittaranjan Das ('Deshbandhu')**.
- **Rise:** as a leader of the Congress **left wing** (those wanting bolder action and socialist economics), he was elected Congress **President at the Haripura Session (1938)**, where he pushed **rapid industrialisation** and a **National Planning Committee**.
- **The Tripuri crisis (1939):** Bose stood for re-election and **defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya**, the candidate Gandhi supported. Gandhi took it personally, saying the defeat was **'more my defeat than his'**.
- **The split:** the Congress **Working Committee** (the party's top executive) would not cooperate with Bose, so he **resigned** the presidency.
- **Result:** in **1939** Bose founded the **Forward Bloc** to bring together the **left-wing and radical elements** inside the Congress for an uncompromising fight for freedom.

## Picture it (timeline)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1938 | Bose elected President at Haripura |
| 1939 | Re-elected at Tripuri (beats Sitaramayya) → resigns |
| 1939 | Founds the Forward Bloc |

## Terms explained

- **ICS (Indian Civil Service)** — the top administrative service under the British; Bose resigned from it.
- **Deshbandhu** — 'Friend of the Nation', the title of C.R. Das, Bose's mentor.
- **Congress left wing** — leaders favouring bolder, often socialist, action.
- **Working Committee** — the small executive body that runs the Congress day to day.
- **Forward Bloc** — the party Bose founded in 1939 inside the Congress.

**Don't confuse** — Bose was **President twice** (1938 and 1939); the clash with Gandhi was at **Tripuri (1939)**, not Haripura.

**Remember it** — 'HT': **H**aripura (1938) then **T**ripuri (1939) — and at T he beat Sitaramayya, then quit.

**TL;DR**

- Bose resigned the ICS; mentored by C.R. Das; led the Congress left.
- President at Haripura (1938) and Tripuri (1939).
- At Tripuri beat Gandhi's candidate Sitaramayya ('more my defeat than his'), then resigned.
- Founded the Forward Bloc (1939).
keyPoints: Bose (b. 1897, Cuttack) resigned the ICS and became a protégé of C.R. Das in Bengal.
Elected Congress President at Haripura (1938), backing planning and industrialisation.
At Tripuri (1939) he defeated Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya, then resigned.
Gandhi called Sitaramayya's defeat 'more my defeat than his'.
He founded the Forward Bloc in 1939 to unite Congress's left wing.
items.mnemonic: Bose's two chairs: 'HT' = Haripura (1938) then Tripuri (1939).
items.source: NCERT & Britannica — Subhas Chandra Bose; Haripura & Tripuri sessions

items.title: Netaji: Escape, the INA & Azad Hind
items.body:
**In one line** — The dramatic story of Bose's wartime escape abroad, his revival of the Indian National Army, and the Azad Hind government that fought the British by force.

**Why it is asked** — The route (Germany then Japan), who first raised the INA (Mohan Singh), the women's regiment, the Moirang flag, and the slogans are all repeat facts.

## The story

- **The Great Escape (1941):** placed under house arrest in Calcutta, Bose **slipped away in 1941** and reached **Germany via Afghanistan and the USSR**. There he raised the **Free India Legion** and set up a **Free India Centre**.
- **The submarine voyage (1943):** to reach Japanese-held **Southeast Asia**, Bose made a famous **submarine journey** — transferring from a German U-boat to a Japanese submarine mid-ocean.
- **The INA (Azad Hind Fauj):** the Indian National Army was first raised from Indian **prisoners of war** by **Mohan Singh in 1942**, then **revived and reorganised by Bose in 1943**. Its women's wing was the **Rani of Jhansi Regiment**, led by **Capt. Lakshmi Sahgal**.
- **On Indian soil:** fighting alongside Japan, the INA reached India's north-east and **hoisted the Indian flag at Moirang, Manipur, in 1944**.
- **Azad Hind Government:** Bose proclaimed the **Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind)** at **Singapore in October 1943**, recognised by several Axis powers; it even had its own currency and briefly administered the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
- **Slogans & end:** Bose gave India **'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom'** and **'Jai Hind'**, and is revered as **'Netaji'** (respected leader). He is reported to have **died in an air crash at Taihoku (Taipei) in August 1945**; his birthday, **23 January**, is now **Parakram Diwas**.

## Picture it (route & timeline)

| When | What |
|---|---|
| 1941 | Escape from Calcutta → Germany (Free India Legion) |
| 1943 | Submarine to SE Asia; revives INA; Azad Hind Govt (Singapore, Oct) |
| 1944 | INA at Imphal/Kohima; flag at Moirang, Manipur |
| Aug 1945 | Reported air crash at Taihoku |

## Terms explained

- **Free India Legion** — the unit of Indian volunteers Bose raised in Germany.
- **INA / Azad Hind Fauj** — the Indian National Army that fought the British with Japanese help.
- **Prisoners of war (PoWs)** — captured soldiers; the first INA was formed from Indian PoWs.
- **Netaji** — 'respected leader', Bose's popular title.
- **Parakram Diwas** — 'Day of Valour', observed on Bose's birthday, 23 January.

**Don't confuse** — the **INA was first raised by Mohan Singh (1942)**; Bose **revived** it in 1943. The flag was hoisted at **Moirang in 1944**, not at Kohima in 1942.

**Remember it** — Bose's route 'G then J': **G**ermany first, then **J**apan/Southeast Asia (by submarine, 1943).

**TL;DR**

- 1941 escape to Germany (Free India Legion); 1943 submarine to SE Asia.
- INA first raised by Mohan Singh (1942), revived by Bose (1943); Rani of Jhansi Regiment (Capt. Lakshmi Sahgal).
- Flag hoisted at Moirang, Manipur (1944); Azad Hind Govt at Singapore (Oct 1943).
- Slogans 'Give me blood…', 'Jai Hind'; 'Netaji'; reported 1945 Taihoku crash; 23 Jan = Parakram Diwas.
keyPoints: Bose escaped house arrest in 1941 and reached Germany, raising the Free India Legion.
In 1943 he travelled by submarine to Southeast Asia and revived the INA (first raised by Mohan Singh, 1942).
The Rani of Jhansi Regiment (women's wing) was led by Capt. Lakshmi Sahgal.
The INA hoisted the Indian flag at Moirang, Manipur, in 1944.
Bose proclaimed the Azad Hind Government at Singapore in October 1943.
Slogans 'Give me blood…' and 'Jai Hind'; reported to have died in a 1945 Taihoku air crash; 23 January is Parakram Diwas.
items.mnemonic: Bose's route 'G-J': Germany then Japan/Southeast Asia (by submarine, 1943).
items.source: Britannica & Government of India — Subhas Chandra Bose; INA; Azad Hind Government

items.title: INA Trials, Rash Behari Bose & PYQ Specials
items.body:
**In one line** — The people and events most often tested from this topic: who handed Bose the INA, the Red Fort trials, Patel's Karachi session, and the renamed Andaman islands.

**Why it is asked** — These are direct previous-year-question (PYQ) favourites — the INA trio, the handover date, and the Karachi 1931 resolution appear again and again.

## The story

**Rash Behari Bose & the founding of the INA**
- **Rash Behari Bose**, a veteran revolutionary living in Japan, helped set up the first INA and the **Indian Independence League**, and formally **handed INA leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose on 4 July 1943** at Singapore.

**INA campaigns**
- The INA fought alongside the Japanese at **Imphal and Kohima (1944)** and raised the Indian flag at **Moirang, Manipur**.

**The INA (Red Fort) Trials, 1945**
- After Japan surrendered, captured INA officers were put on trial at the **Red Fort, Delhi (November 1945)**.
- The famous first trial was of three officers chosen as **one Hindu, one Muslim, one Sikh**: **Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon**.
- Their **defence counsel** included **Bhulabhai Desai, Jawaharlal Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru and K.N. Katju**. The trials stirred huge public sympathy and helped spark the **Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Mutiny of 1946**.

**Patel — the Karachi Session (1931)**
- **Sardar Patel presided over the Congress Karachi Session (1931)**, which endorsed the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact** and adopted the landmark resolution on **Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme**.

**Commemoration — Andaman islands**
- The **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** were renamed to honour the INA: **Ross Island → Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep**, and **Neil & Havelock → Shaheed & Swaraj Dweep**.

## Terms explained

- **Indian Independence League** — the overseas Indian body (in East/Southeast Asia) backing the INA.
- **Court-martial** — a military trial of soldiers; here, of INA officers at the Red Fort.
- **RIN Mutiny (1946)** — the revolt of Royal Indian Navy ratings, partly inspired by the INA trials.
- **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** — the agreement that paused Civil Disobedience and freed many prisoners.
- **Dweep** — 'island'; used in the renamed Andaman islands.

**Don't confuse** — **Rash Behari Bose** (who handed over the INA) is a different person from **Subhas Chandra Bose** (Netaji). And **Patel presided at Karachi (1931)**, not at Lahore (that was Nehru).

**Remember it** — Red Fort trio = one each Hindu-Muslim-Sikh: **S**ahgal, **S**hah Nawaz Khan, **D**hillon.

**TL;DR**

- Rash Behari Bose handed INA leadership to S.C. Bose on 4 July 1943.
- INA fought at Imphal/Kohima (1944); flag at Moirang.
- Red Fort Trials (Nov 1945): Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon; defence Desai/Nehru/Sapru/Katju → fed the 1946 RIN Mutiny.
- Patel presided over the Karachi Session (1931): Fundamental Rights + National Economic Programme.
- Andaman renaming: Ross → Netaji Dweep; Neil & Havelock → Shaheed & Swaraj Dweep.
keyPoints: Rash Behari Bose founded the first INA/Indian Independence League and handed leadership to S.C. Bose on 4 July 1943.
INA fought at Imphal & Kohima (1944) and hoisted the flag at Moirang, Manipur.
INA (Red Fort) Trials, Nov 1945: Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon (Hindu-Muslim-Sikh trio).
Defence counsel: Bhulabhai Desai, Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru, K.N. Katju; trials fed the 1946 RIN Mutiny.
Patel presided over the Congress Karachi Session (1931) — Fundamental Rights & National Economic Programme resolution.
Andaman islands renamed: Ross → Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep; Neil & Havelock → Shaheed & Swaraj Dweep.
items.mnemonic: INA trio at Red Fort = one each Hindu-Muslim-Sikh: Sahgal, Shah Nawaz Khan, Dhillon.
items.source: Standard references — INA Red Fort trials; Rash Behari Bose; Karachi Session 1931; Andaman renaming

items.title: For Mains — Patel & Bose
items.body:
**In one line** — For Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-4b: 'Gandhi, Bose, Patel; Ambedkar'), treat Patel and Bose as two contrasting answers to the same question — *how should India win and then hold its freedom?*

**Why it is asked** — Paper-II lists these leaders by name; questions ask you to *assess contribution* and *compare approaches*, not merely narrate biographies.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | Patel | Bose |
|---|---|---|
| Method | Constitutional, organisational, firm statecraft | Militant, armed struggle; tactical Axis help |
| Signature achievement | Integration of ~565 princely states | Revival of the INA & Azad Hind Government |
| Relation to Gandhi | Loyal lieutenant, non-violent | Diverged; valued force over ahimsa |
| Nation-building role | Territorial unity, 'steel frame' civil services | Inspired armed nationalism, mass sympathy |
| Limitation / critique | Centralising; unresolved Kashmir | Axis association debated; strategy failed militarily |
| Legacy today | Statue of Unity, Ekta Diwas, Bharat Ratna 1991 | 'Netaji', Parakram Diwas (23 Jan) |

## Facts / dates to quote

1. **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)** → title 'Sardar'; **Kheda (1918)** first campaign.
2. **~565 princely states**; **Instrument of Accession** (defence, external affairs, communications); **V.P. Menon**.
3. **Junagadh plebiscite (Feb 1948)**, **Hyderabad Operation Polo (Sept 1948)**, **Kashmir accession (26 Oct 1947)**.
4. **Haripura (1938)** & **Tripuri (1939)** presidencies; **Forward Bloc (1939)**.
5. **INA** (Mohan Singh 1942 → Bose 1943), **Azad Hind Govt Singapore (Oct 1943)**, **Moirang flag (1944)**, **Red Fort trials (1945)** → **RIN Mutiny (1946)**.
6. **Karachi Session (1931)** under Patel — Fundamental Rights & National Economic Programme.

## AP angle

The **Tripuri** episode has a direct Andhra link: Bose defeated **Pattabhi Sitaramayya of Andhra**, who later became Congress President (1948) and Governor. Use this to connect the national narrative to AP for Paper-II.

## Use in answers

- **Example to cite:** contrast Patel's bloodless unification of 565 states with Bose's armed INA to show two models of nationalism in one line.
- **Quote idea:** Patel's **'steel frame'** for administration; Gandhi's **'more my defeat than his'** for the Tripuri clash.
- **Diagram idea:** a two-column compare table (Patel vs Bose: method · achievement · legacy) to structure a 15-mark answer.

**TL;DR**

- Frame Patel and Bose as contrasting nationalisms: statecraft vs armed struggle.
- Keep integration facts (565, Instrument of Accession, J-H-K) and INA facts (1942/1943, Azad Hind, Red Fort) ready.
- Use the Pattabhi Sitaramayya link for the AP angle; end with their complementary legacies.
keyPoints: Mains clause M2-4b (Gandhi, Bose, Patel; Ambedkar), Paper-II; questions ask for assessment and comparison.
Patel = constitutional statecraft, integration of ~565 states, 'steel frame'; Bose = armed struggle, INA, Azad Hind.
Quote dates: Bardoli 1928, Instrument of Accession, J-H-K; Haripura 1938/Tripuri 1939, Forward Bloc 1939; INA 1943, Red Fort 1945.
AP angle: Tripuri clash was against Pattabhi Sitaramayya of Andhra (Congress President 1948).
Structure answers with a Patel-vs-Bose compare table and complementary-legacy conclusion.
